prompt: I have about 8,000 hiking trail segments stored as GeoJSON, and users need to click a trail to see its name and distance. I also need a basemap showing terrain and roads. How should I set up the data sources in MapLibre — do I need vector tiles, or can I use GeoJSON?

Description: implicit — dataset outgrew GeoJSON without the user naming tiles
prompt: My parcel layer is a 180 MB GeoJSON file with around 400,000 polygons. The browser hangs for ages on load and sometimes the tab just dies. I've already tried minifying the JSON. What now?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR  
A 180 MB / ≈ 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is far beyond the practical limits of MapLibre’s **`geojson`** source. The browser has to download the whole file, parse it into JavaScript objects, and then build a WebGL buffer for every vertex – that’s why it hangs or crashes.  

**The fix is to stop sending the whole GeoJSON to the client and serve the data as tiles.**  
1. **Simplify & compress** the geometry (optional but makes the tile-generation step cheaper).  
2. **Generate vector tiles** (MVT/MLT) from the simplified GeoJSON.  
3. Host the tiles (e.g. as a PMTiles archive, an MBTiles/TileJSON endpoint, or a cloud-native tile service).  
4. Add the tile source to your MapLibre style as a **`vector`** source and draw your polygons with a layer that sits above the basemap.

Below is a step-by-step checklist, the tools you can use, and a few “quick-win” tricks if you need something temporary.

---

## 1. Why GeoJSON is no longer viable

| Metric | GeoJSON limits (practical) | Your file |
|--------|----------------------------|-----------|
| File size | **< 2 MB** (smooth) – **5–20 MB** (noticeable lag) – **> 50 MB** (high crash risk) | **180 MB** |
| Feature count | **< 5 k** (sweet spot) – **≈ 50 k** (slow) – **> 100 k** (crash zone) | **≈ 400 k** |
| Browser work | One big download + full parse + full vertex buffer | All of the above, multiplied by 400 k polygons |

Even if you minify the JSON, the browser still has to allocate memory for every coordinate pair. The only way to keep the map responsive is to **serve only the data that is actually visible** – that’s exactly what vector tiles do.

---

## 2. Quick-win “client-side tiling” (only for prototyping)

If you need a *temporary* solution while you set up a tile pipeline, you can let the browser tile the GeoJSON on-the-fly with **`geojson-vt`** (or the MapLibre-built-in `GeoJSONSource` with `cluster: true` for points).  

```js
import geojsonvt from 'geojson-vt';
import {GeoJSONSource} from 'maplibre-gl';

const tileIndex = geojsonvt(largeGeojson, {
  maxZoom: 14,          // highest zoom you’ll display
  tolerance: 3,         // higher = more simplification
  extent: 4096,         // default tile extent
});

map.addSource('my-data', {
  type: 'geojson',
  data: {
    // a tiny wrapper that asks geojson-vt for the right tile
    getTile: (z, x, y) => tileIndex.getTile(z, x, y)
  }
});
```

**Caveats**

* Still loads the whole 180 MB file once – you’ll still see the initial freeze.  
* No server-side caching, so every client repeats the work.  
* Not suitable for production or mobile users.

**Bottom line:** Use this only to prototype the visual style while you spin up a real tile service.

---

## 3. Proper solution – generate **vector tiles** (MVT/MLT)

### 3.1. Geometry preparation (optional but recommended)

| Goal | Tool | One-liner example |
|------|------|-------------------|
| **Simplify polygons** (reduce vertex count, keep topology) | **mapshaper** (`-simplify dp <percentage>`) | `mapshaper input.geojson -simplify dp 5% -o output.geojson` |
| **Reduce coordinate precision** (e.g. 6-decimal places ≈ 0.1 m) | **mapshaper** (`-precision 6`) | `mapshaper input.geojson -precision 6 -o output.geojson` |
| **Convert to TopoJSON** (shared line strings) – can shrink size dramatically for line-heavy data | **topojson** (`-simplify-proportion`) | `topojson -o output.topojson --simplify-proportion 0.05 input.geojson` |

You can chain these steps (`mapshaper … -simplify … -precision … -o …`) to get a much smaller source file (often 10-30 % of the original size) before tiling. The simplification level should be chosen per zoom level; the tile generator will automatically re-simplify for lower zooms.

### 3.2. Tile generation tools

| Tool | What it does | Typical workflow | Docs |
|------|--------------|------------------|------|
| **tippecanoe** (C, fast, works on any GeoJSON) | Generates **MBTiles** (MVT) from one or many GeoJSON files; automatically creates zoom-dependent simplifications. | `tippecanoe -o mydata.mbtiles --maximum-zoom=14 --minimum-zoom=5 --drop-densest-as-needed --simplify-only-low-zooms input.geojson` | <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe> |
| **Planetiler** (Java/Kotlin, OSM-centric but works with any GeoJSON) | High-performance pipeline that can read GeoParquet, FlatGeobuf, etc., and output **MLT** (MapLibre Tile) or MVT. | `java -jar planetiler.jar --input input.geojson --output mydata.pmtiles` | <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler> |
| **tilemaker** (C++) | Simple conversion from OSM PBF to vector tiles; can also ingest GeoJSON via `ogr2ogr` first. | `tilemaker --input input.geojson --output mydata.mbtiles` | <https://github.com/systemed/tilemaker> |
| **ogr2ogr → PMTiles** (GDAL) | GDAL 3.8+ can write directly to **PMTiles** (`-f PMTiles`). | `ogr2ogr -f PMTiles mydata.pmtiles input.geojson -dsco MAXZOOM=14` | <https://gdal.org/drivers/vector/pmtiles.html> |

> **Do not write the full build script here** – just point the user to the official docs for each tool. The skill’s policy says we should *name* the tools and link to their documentation, not provide a custom pipeline.

### 3.3. Hosting the tiles

| Hosting option | When it makes sense | Quick start |
|----------------|--------------------|-------------|
| **Static file server (e.g. GitHub Pages, Netlify, S3)** + **TileJSON** | Small-to-medium MBTiles (≤ 1 GB) that can be served as individual `.pbf` files (tippecanoe can `--output-dir`). | `tippecanoe … --output-dir ./tiles && npx tilejson-cli ./tiles > tilejson.json` |
| **PMTiles archive** + **`maplibre-pmtiles-patterns`** skill | One-file distribution, offline kiosks, or when you want HTTP-range-request serving without a tile server. | `pmtiles create mydata.pmtiles ./tiles` then serve the `.pmtiles` file via any static host; MapLibre reads it with `pmtiles://` protocol. |
| **Tile server (TileServer GL, Tileserver-PHP, t-rex, or Cloud-native services like MapTiler Cloud, AWS OpenData Tiles)** | Larger datasets, need CORS, caching, or dynamic styling. | Deploy the MBTiles/PMTiles to the server; it will expose `/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`. |
| **Cloud-native vector tile services (e.g. Amazon S3 + CloudFront, Azure Blob + CDN)** | When you already store data in object storage and want edge caching. | Upload the individual `.pbf` tiles (or the PMTiles file) and configure a CDN to serve them with proper `Cache-Control`. |

**Pick the simplest thing that works for you now** – for a one-off demo, a static folder of `.pbf` tiles (generated by tippecanoe with `--output-dir`) is the fastest to get up and running.

---

## 4. Wiring the vector source in MapLibre

```javascript
// 1️⃣ Add the vector source (TileJSON or PMTiles URL)
map.addSource('my-polygons', {
  type: 'vector',
  // If you have a TileJSON file:
  // url: 'https://example.com/tilejson.json',
  // If you are using a PMTiles archive:
  url: 'pmtiles://https://example.com/mydata.pmtiles',
  // optional: set minzoom / maxzoom to match what you generated
  minzoom: 5,
  maxzoom: 14
});

// 2️⃣ Add a layer that draws the polygons
map.addLayer({
  id: 'my-polygons-fill',
  type: 'fill',
  source: 'my-polygons',
  'source-layer': 'mydata',   // name of the layer inside the tileset (tippecanoe defaults to the filename)
  paint: {
    'fill-color': '#0066ff',
    'fill-opacity': 0.4,
    'fill-outline-color': '#003399'
  }
});
```

*If you already have a basemap style URL (e.g. from MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, or a custom style), add the above source **in addition** to the basemap. Insert your layer **before** the first symbol layer if you want your polygons to appear under labels.*  
(See the **`maplibre-source-wiring`** skill for exact layer-order tricks.)

---

## 5. What if you truly need a *single* file (offline kiosk, air-gapped demo)?

The only legitimate case for bundling everything into one source is **offline use**. In that scenario:

1. Generate a **PMTiles** archive that contains **both** the basemap vector tiles *and* your data tiles (you can concatenate two MBTiles files with `pmtiles merge`).  
2. Serve the archive locally (file:// or a tiny static server).  
3. Use the same `pmtiles://` URL in the style.  

Even then, keep the basemap and your data in **separate source names** inside the style – MapLibre will request them concurrently from the same archive, and you still retain the ability to toggle layers on/off.

---

## 6. Checklist – from “my map hangs” to “my map runs”

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| **1** | **Simplify** the GeoJSON (mapshaper – `-simplify dp 5%` or similar). |
| **2** | **Generate vector tiles** with `tippecanoe` (or Planetiler) – target `maxzoom` that matches your UI (e.g., 14). |
| **3** | **Host** the tiles (static folder of `.pbf` files, a PMTiles archive, or a tile server). |
| **4** | **Add a `vector` source** to your MapLibre style, referencing the TileJSON/PMTiles URL. |
| **5** | **Create a layer** that draws the polygons; place it appropriately in the draw order. |
| **6** | **Test** on a low-end device (mobile, old laptop). If still slow, increase the simplification tolerance or lower `maxzoom`. |
| **7** | **Optional** – If you need *dynamic* updates, generate new tiles on the server side and replace the MBTiles/PMTiles file; the client will fetch the new tiles automatically. |

Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer – you don’t need a “single-source” tileset for performance.**  
MapLibre can request any number of sources in parallel, and a style that mixes a hosted basemap (vector tiles) with your own data (GeoJSON or a separate vector-tile source) is the standard, low-maintenance pattern.  

Below is a concise guide that:

1. **Explains why the “one source” idea isn’t a performance win**  
2. **Shows the recommended two-source pattern**  
3. **Lists the tools you would use if you *must* bake everything into one tileset** (without giving a step-by-step build script).  

---

## 1️⃣ Why a single combined tileset isn’t a performance optimization

| Concern | Reality with separate sources | Reality with a single combined tileset |
|---------|------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Network cost** | MapLibre opens parallel HTTP connections to each source; the total bytes transferred are the same as the sum of the individual tiles. | Same total bytes, but you lose the ability to cache the basemap independently (basemap tiles are reused across many apps). |
| **Update frequency** | You can republish only your delivery-zone tiles when they change. | Any change to your polygons forces a full rebuild of the whole OSM-plus-your-data tileset (potentially millions of tiles). |
| **Attribution & licensing** | You keep the basemap provider’s attribution separate and stay compliant with OSM’s Share-Alike. | You become a redistributor of OSM data; you must carry the basemap’s attribution and license on every tile you serve. |
| **Styling flexibility** | Styles can be swapped or tweaked without touching the data tiles (e.g., switch from a light to a dark basemap). | Styling changes require a new tile build or a completely new style layer on top of the same tiles. |
| **Complexity** | Only two sources to configure in the style JSON. | You need a custom tile-generation pipeline, CI/CD for rebuilds, and storage for a much larger tile archive. |

Because MapLibre already fetches all declared sources concurrently, there is **no per-source rendering penalty** to avoid. Published basemap styles routinely declare 3-5 vector sources themselves (roads, water, landcover, labels, etc.) and the browser handles them without issue.

**Bottom line:** Use a *basemap source* + a *your-data source* unless you have a very specific offline-only or kiosk use-case where a single file is required.

---

## 2️⃣ Recommended “two-source” setup (the simplest, most maintainable)

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "basemap": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "https://example.com/tiles/basemap.json"   // TileJSON from a provider (OpenStreetMap, MapTiler, etc.)
    },
    "deliveryZones": {
      "type": "geojson",               // or "vector" if you pre-tile them
      "data": "/data/delivery-zones.geojson"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    // 1️⃣ Insert your delivery-zone layer *before* the first symbol layer
    //    so your polygons sit under road/label symbols.
    {
      "id": "delivery-zones-fill",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "deliveryZones",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#ff8800", "fill-opacity": 0.3 }
    },
    // 2️⃣ Then add the rest of the basemap layers (or just reference the
    //    style URL you got from the provider, which already contains them).
    //    No need to copy OSM layers into your style.
    //    Example: you could just set `"style": "https://example.com/basemap/style.json"`
  ]
}
```

*If you prefer your delivery zones as vector tiles (e.g., to keep the same binary format as the basemap), generate a tiny tile set just for those polygons and reference it with `type: "vector"` and a `url` to its TileJSON. The rest of the style stays unchanged.*

---

## 3️⃣ How you **could** merge OSM data with your polygons into one tileset  

> **Only follow this path if you truly need a single archive** (offline kiosk, demo that must work without any network, or a very constrained environment).  

### The high-level pipeline (no detailed commands)

| Step | What you do | Typical tool(s) |
|------|--------------|-----------------|
| **A. Get an OSM extract** | Download the region you need (e.g., a `.osm.pbf` for your country or state). | `osmconvert`, `osmfilter`, or simply fetch from Geofabrik. |
| **B. Prepare your delivery-zone polygons** | Convert them to GeoJSON (or another vector-tile-friendly format) and, if needed, simplify them to keep tile size reasonable. | `ogr2ogr`, `mapshaper` (simplify), or any GIS tool you already use. |
| **C. Merge the two datasets** | Concatenate the OSM features with your polygons into a single GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf/GeoParquet file. | `ogr2ogr -append`, `tippecanoe`’s `--merge` flag, or a custom script (Python/Node). |
| **D. Tile-generation** | Turn the merged vector data into vector tiles (MVT or the newer MLT). | **Tippecanoe** (for GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf) or **Planetiler** (for OSM-style pipelines). |
| **E. Publish TileJSON** | Create a TileJSON document that points to the tile URL pattern (`/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`). | `tilejson-cli` or manual JSON edit. |
| **F. Host the tiles** | Serve the `.pbf` files via a static file server, CDN, or a lightweight tile server (e.g., `tileserver-gl`, `pmtiles` with `maplibre-pmtiles-patterns`). | Any HTTP server, Cloudflare Workers, or S3 + CloudFront. |
| **G. Update the style** | Reference the single source in your style JSON (`type: "vector", url: "https://…/tileset.json"`). | Same style you would use for a basemap, just one source. |

#### Tools you’ll likely need

| Tool | What it does | Docs |
|------|--------------|------|
| **Tippecanoe** | Fast command-line generator for MVT from GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf. Handles simplification, zoom-level control, and attribute filtering. | <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe> |
| **Planetiler** | Java/Kotlin pipeline that reads OSM PBF, lets you write custom feature processors, and outputs vector tiles (MVT or MLT). Good for large-scale OSM + custom data merges. | <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler> |
| **ogr2ogr / GDAL** | Convert between GIS formats, reproject, clip, and merge layers. | <https://gdal.org/programs/ogr2ogr.html> |
| **mapshaper** | Simplify and clean GeoJSON/TopoJSON on the command line or in the browser. | <https://github.com/mbloch/mapshaper> |
| **tileserver-gl** or **PMTiles** | Serve the generated `.pbf` tiles via HTTP/HTTPS. | <https://github.com/klokantech/tileserver-gl> ; <https://github.com/protomaps/PMTiles> |
| **TileJSON generator** | Small utility to emit a TileJSON file from a tile directory. | <https://github.com/mapbox/tilejson-cli> |

### Important caveats when you merge OSM with your data

1. **Attribution & licensing** – OSM data is under ODbL. If you redistribute a combined tileset, you must include the OSM attribution and make the source data (or a derivative) available under the same license.  
2. **Tile size** – Adding polygons to a full-planet OSM tileset can blow up tile sizes dramatically. Use `--drop-densest-as-needed` (Tippecanoe) or custom zoom-level simplification in Planetiler to keep each tile < 200 KB (ideal for web).  
3. **Feature IDs** – Preserve unique IDs for your delivery zones if you need click/hover queries; otherwise they may be re-indexed during tiling.  
4. **Re-building** – Any edit to your polygons forces a full re-run of the pipeline (or at least a regional rebuild). Plan a CI job that triggers on GeoJSON changes.  
5. **Performance testing** – After the first build, load the style in a dev page and watch the Network tab. If any tile exceeds ~200 KB or you see long “waiting” times at high zoom, revisit simplification or consider splitting your data back into a separate source.

---

## 4️⃣ TL;DR – What you should do today

1. **Pick a hosted vector basemap** (e.g., MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, or a self-hosted OSM vector tileset).  
2. **Add your delivery-zone polygons as a separate source** – start with a plain GeoJSON source; if you hit the 2 MB / 5 k-feature sweet spot limit, switch to a tiny vector-tile source generated with Tippecanoe.  
3. **Insert your layer before the first symbol layer** so labels stay on top.  
4. **Only consider a single combined tileset** if you have a hard offline requirement; then use Tippecanoe or Planetiler as outlined above, and be prepared for the licensing and rebuild overhead.

---

### Quick “starter” commands (just for reference – not a full pipeline)

```bash
# 1️⃣ Get a regional OSM extract (example: state of Ohio)
wget https://download.geofabrik.de/north-america/us/ohio-latest.osm.pbf -O ohio.osm.pbf

# 2️⃣ Convert your delivery zones to GeoJSON (if they are in Shapefile)
ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON delivery_zones.geojson delivery_zones.shp

# 3️⃣ Merge OSM + your polygons into one GeoJSON (Tippecanoe can read multiple files)
#    Tippecanoe will automatically concatenate them.
tippecanoe \
  --output=combined.mbtiles \
  --layer=osm \
  --layer=delivery_zones \
  --drop-densest-as-needed \
  --maximum-zoom=14 \
  ohio.osm.pbf delivery_zones.geojson

# 4️⃣ Serve the MBTiles with PMTiles (optional)
pmtiles convert combined.mbtiles combined.pmtiles
# Then host `combined.pmtiles` with a static server or Cloudflare Workers.
```

*These commands are illustrative; you’ll need to tune zoom levels, layer names, and attribute filtering for your specific use case.*

---

## 5️⃣ Further reading

- **Tippecanoe docs** – command-line options for simplification, layer naming, and zoom control.  
- **Planetiler docs** – how to write a custom feature processor that injects your polygons into the OSM pipeline.  
- **MapLibre Style Spec – sources** – how to declare multiple sources and control layer order.  
- **OSM licensing FAQ** – what you must include when redistributing OSM-derived tiles.  

---

**In short:** Use a basemap source + a separate delivery-zone source. Only build a single combined tileset if you truly need an offline-only artifact, and then rely on Tippecanoe or Planetiler to do the heavy lifting. This keeps your workflow simple, your tiles small, and your licensing clean. Happy mapping!
